newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - British mandarin haunts Patten's HK handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British mandarin haunts Patten's HK handover.

text.p: One man was a conservative scholar-bureaucrat whose governing style was modelled on the ancient dictates of Chinese Confucianism.
The other is a professional politician with a reformer's zeal who introduced new levels of democracy to one of the last jewels of European empire in the Far East.
At first glance, the mandarin who ruled the eastern Chinese port of Weihaiwei from 1927 to 1930 and the last Hong Kong governor might seem to have little in common.

But for all the decades that separate them and the differences in their governing styles, the responsibility shouldered by both men was the same -- to be the final British ruler of a territory wrested from China by London's 19th century imperial might.

Chris Patten will go down in history as the man who charted Hong Kong's course in the years leading up to its return to Beijing rule on July 1, but the road from British rule to Chinese sovereignty was trod by Reginald Johnston long before.

As commissioner of the treaty port of Weihaiwei, Johnston -- a Chinese-speaking sinologist who had been a tutor to China's last emperor -- presided over a handover of power that might be the envy of any imperial administrator.
A HEART AS CLEAR AS PURE WATER
On October 1, 1930, Johnston returned Weihaiwei to the Chinese motherland in a ceremony full of military parades and big gun salutes that he had carefully planned himself.

A local Chinese businessman praised British officials as having "loved the people", and incoming Chinese administrators admitted that Johnston and his predecessors had ruled wisely and well, wrote scholar Pamela Atwell in a history of Weihaiwei.

Residents had earlier feted the departing Scottish mandarin, whose Chinese studies had imbued him with a deep respect for local Confucian traditions, and had presented him with farewell scrolls and a traditional porcelain bowl of clear water.

"The ordinary people had a very high opinion of Mr Johnston ...(they) thought his heart was as clear as pure water; you could see to the very bottom of it," said local historian Liu Deyu in a interview in the port now known as Weihai city.
British rule intruded little on the lives of the farmers and fishermen of Weihaiwei, the oldest of whom remember their one-time overlords without apparent bitterness.
"When the British were here things were very relaxed," said retired fisherman Li Wenqing, 88. "There were few controls."

Johnston considered the key to successful leadership in Weihaiwei, leased in 1898 by Britain from the decaying Qing dynasty (1644-1911), to be conscious emulation of the methods of China's scholar officials.

"To regard Weihaiwei as an example of the English power of successfully ruling hordes of alien subjects shows a misapprehension of the facts," he wrote during an early stint in the backward territory, once dubbed the "Cinderella of the British Empire".
A GO-GETTING GOVERNOR
The contrast between Johnston and Chris Patten, Hong Kong's 28th and final British governor, could hardly be greater.
Johnston was a career colonialist, an accomplished scholar of Chinese who had spent six years in Beijing's Forbidden City tutoring the last emperor, Pu Yi.
Patten came to Hong Kong raw from the political rough and tumble of British politics, where he had lost his seat in parliament in the 1992 general election.

Within months of his arrival in Britain's last Asian outpost, the new governor found himself heading for conflict with China, which furiously rejected the political reforms he launched in response to popular demands for more democracy.
Beijing-backed newspapers showered Patten with abuse, denouncing him as a "dictator", "political prostitute", "serpent" and "criminal for 10,000 years".
Local businessmen accused him of jeopardising economic stability and even pro-democracy campaigners turned on Patten when the limits of Hong Kong's political reform became clear.
All that Chinese officials have promised the governor for the final midnight handover ceremony is a handshake. Warm words of praise seem unlikely. A bowl of clear water even less so.
LIGHT HAND MEANS LITTLE LEGACY

While the light hand of Johnston's rule in Weihaiwei won praise in 1930, the support many Hong Kong residents still accord their last governor suggests they see his activist approach as more suited to the 1990s.
And while Patten's clashes with China have been mainly disputes over how to safeguard Hong Kong's future freedoms, historians say Weihaiwei's British rulers had few such concerns.
Indeed, Johnston's conservatism put him far out of step with reform-minded Chinese counterparts and may have helped to hinder Weihaiwei's economic development.
Officials in modern Weihai city say 32 years of British rule created only a meagre architectural and economic legacy.
"They did not build much while they were here," said one city official. "It was different from Hong Kong."
